question: Britannia buys ₹50 Cr of wheat flour in March 2024 to make biscuits. By March 31, only ₹35 Cr worth of flour has been used in biscuits that were sold during the year. Under the matching principle, what amount should be recorded as Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) in FY24?
before: The matching principle states that expenses must be recorded in the same period as the revenues they helped generate. Britannia generated revenue from biscuits made using ₹35 Cr of flour, so only ₹35 Cr is the matched expense for FY24. The remaining ₹15 Cr of flour stays on the balance sheet as Inventory (a current asset) and becomes COGS only when the future biscuits are sold. Option A is wrong because expensing the full purchase ignores matching and would distort margins. Option C is the inventory value, not the COGS. Option D is wrong because the consumed portion absolutely should be recognised. This is the same logic that drives depreciation — costs are spread to match the revenue they generate.
after:
Concept: The matching principle requires that expenses be recorded in the same accounting period as the revenues they help generate, not when cash is paid or goods are purchased.

Why this is correct: Britannia sold biscuits in FY24 that used ₹35 Cr of flour. Under the matching principle, only the flour consumed in generating FY24 revenue qualifies as COGS for that year. The remaining ₹15 Cr of flour has not yet contributed to any sale, so it remains on the balance sheet as Inventory and will become COGS only in the period when those biscuits are sold.

Why the others are wrong:

A (₹50 Cr — full purchase amount): This violates the matching principle by expensing the entire purchase in FY24 even though ₹15 Cr of flour has not yet generated any revenue. This would overstate COGS and understate profit for FY24, and understate COGS in future periods when the remaining flour is actually used.

C (₹15 Cr — the unused flour): This confuses the portion that remains as an asset with the portion that should be expensed. The ₹15 Cr is the inventory value that stays on the balance sheet, not an expense to be recorded as COGS.

D (Nothing, because the flour will be used next year): This ignores that ₹35 Cr of the flour was already consumed to produce biscuits sold in FY24. The matching principle demands recognition of this cost against FY24 revenue, regardless of when the remaining stock is used.

Intuition: In equity research, COGS accuracy is critical because it directly drives gross margin and operating leverage analysis. Blindly matching all purchases to the purchase year would create false margin swings whenever inventory levels change, making it impossible to see true operational performance. The matching principle forces consistency: costs flow to P&L only when the revenues they enabled actually materialise.
